title: How to find a billion-dollar startup idea: avoid mimesis, use your unique experience, notice gaps
summary: Garry Tan argues most founders copy whatever is already successful (photo sharing, travel plans, local events) because desire is mimetic. Real breakout ideas come from unusual personal experience (Flexport, Patreon), start as toys, and are found by working on hard problems while noting gaps and anomalies.

principles.text: Don't copy the ideas that are already hot; desire is mimetic and crowds produce infinite competition.
principles.quote: Everyone's making the same photo-sharing, podcasting, travel plans, local event apps. Probably because desire is mimetic. We want what other people want.

principles.text: Great startup ideas look like toys at the start, so lack of obvious fame is not a signal against an idea.
principles.quote: the most famous startups were not famous at the moment when they were started.

principles.text: Your unique, different experiences are the raw material for innovative connections and a winning idea.
principles.quote: What makes you new, different and unique in the world will be the exact thing that makes you succeed.

principles.text: Look for founders and ideas rooted in deep, intimate knowledge of a domain, like Ryan Petersen's supply chain experience behind Flexport.
principles.quote: My favorite pitch meetings are with founders who teach you something about the world you didn't know before.

principles.text: You don't need to be novel, but if there's competition you must be clearly better, faster or cheaper.
principles.quote: if there's competition, you have to be better, faster, cheaper in order to stand a chance. Competition is not your friend.

principles.text: The first version can be imperfect; disruptive tech often undershoots user needs before improving rapidly.
principles.quote: it's also okay if the first version of your startup is not quite perfect.
